# Agent Use Cases

Build products with autonomous AI agents using the Wiro API.

## See These Use Cases on the Web

Wiro publishes interactive, fullscreen showcases for the most common agent use cases. Each one walks through a real product story end-to-end (build, deploy, daily operation, brand-voice authoring, scheduled autopilot, and a self-healing climax under an upstream API break), so you can see what the patterns below look like before writing any code.

Showcase | What you'll see 
---|---
Ad Campaign Manager | Drape Studio (bespoke tailoring) running Google Ads + Meta Ads on autopilot: Brand Voice + Budget Control as plain-English skills, AI video ads, OAuth publish, Day-3 auto-pause, weekly review, and a self-heal under the Google Ads API v14 sunset. 
App Event Manager | Nova (creative video + effects app): Calendarific holiday scan across 7 markets, Nano Banana Pro dual-aspect covers, multi-language event copy, App Store Connect publish, autonomous monthly briefing, self-heal under a 503. 
App Review Replies | Prism (photo + video editor): App Store + Google Play replies, Brand Voice + Reply Policy markdown skills, multilingual drafts, dev-team Slack escalation for 1★ crashes, monthly sentiment report, self-heal under token expiry. 
Barber Booking | Scissor Hands salon: WhatsApp + Google Calendar bookings, multi-staff routing with role-based privacy, customer memory, scheduled daily/monthly digests, self-heal under a Calendar API break. 
Customer Win-Back | Swift Sweep (chimney + fireplace service): HubSpot CRM segmentation, Brand Voice + Customer Scorer + Seasonal Reminder as markdown skills, AI seasonal covers, batch WhatsApp send, scheduled autumn run, self-heal under a HubSpot v2 → v3 contacts API deprecation. 
Ecommerce Listings | Coral & Crest (swimwear): 5 Wiro AI models (Virtual Try-On, Product-on-Model, Background Remover, Cover Image, Description), multilingual copy, auto-publish to WordPress + Instagram + Shopify, 84-product Google-Drive bulk-autonomy climax. 
Restaurant Reviews | Green Bottle Coffee: daily chat-based approvals, scheduled reports, anomaly dispatch, self-heal under a Reviews API deprecation. The "no pitch deck required" demo. 

You can also browse every available pre-built agent at wiro.ai/agents/browse (the visual mirror ofPOST /Agent/List). Each agent template has its own marketing page at wiro.ai/agents/{slug} (for example wiro.ai/agents/social-manager, wiro.ai/agents/voice-receptionist, or wiro.ai/agents/blog-content-editor) with screenshots, default skills, credential requirements, and live tier pricing. The full URL for each agent in the Available Agents table below is https://wiro.ai/agents/{slug}.

## Two Deployment Patterns

Every product built on Wiro agents follows one of two patterns. Choosing the right one depends on whether your users need to connect their own third-party accounts.

### Pattern 1: Instance Per Customer

Most agents interact with external services: posting to social media, managing ad campaigns, sending emails. These require OAuth tokens or API keys that belong to the end user. Deploy a separate agent instance for each of your customers.

Why: Each customer connects their own accounts. Credentials are bound to the instance, isolated from other customers.

How: CallPOST /UserAgent/Deploy once per customer, then use the OAuth flow to connect their accounts.

#### Real-World Examples

Your Product | Agent Type | Why Per-Customer 
---|---|---
Digital marketing agency dashboard | Social Manager | Each client connects their own Twitter, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, LinkedIn 
Mobile app company | App Review Support | Each app has its own App Store / Google Play credentials 
E-commerce platform | Google Ads Manager + Meta Ads Manager | Each advertiser connects their own ad accounts 
Marketing SaaS | Newsletter Manager | Each customer connects their own Brevo/SendGrid/Mailchimp 
Sales platform | Lead Generation Manager | Each sales team connects their own Apollo/Lemlist 
Content agency tool | Blog Content Editor | Each client connects their own WordPress site 
App publisher platform | App Event Manager | Each app has its own App Store credentials 
Mobile app publisher | Push Notification Manager | Each app has its own Firebase service account 
Customer engagement tool | Social Manager | Each brand manages their own social presence 
Phone-receptionist platform for SMBs | Voice Receptionist | Each business has its own Twilio number, HubSpot CRM, and Google Calendar 
Video marketing tool or agency | Video Creator | Each client brings its own site, brand and test logins, and pays its model runs from its own Wiro project 

### Pattern 2: Session Per User

For conversational agents that don't need per-user credentials. One agent instance serves many users, each identified by a uniquesessionkey that isolates their conversation history.

Why: No third-party accounts to connect. The agent answers questions using its built-in knowledge or pre-configured data sources.

How: Deploy one instance viaPOST /UserAgent/Deploy, then send messages with different sessionkey values per user.

Aboutsessionkey: This field is optional. If omitted, messages go into a shared "default" session. Reuse the same sessionkey to continue a conversation (the agent retrieves prior messages as context). Use a fresh UUID to start a new conversation. The common convention is one sessionkey per end-user (e.g. "user-456"), but you can also use it per-thread (e.g. "ticket-2025-0817") for products that group conversations by topic. See the Agent Messaging guide for how sessions work. The session key is a label, not a WebSocket channel: you follow a turn with its agenttoken and a session with the sessiontoken from Message/History (see Agent WebSocket).

#### Real-World Examples

Your Product | Use Case | Why Sessions 
---|---|---
Knowledge base chatbot | Answer questions from documentation | No per-user credentials needed 
Product recommendation advisor | Suggest products based on conversation | Same catalog for all users 
Internal company assistant | HR policies, IT help, onboarding | Shared knowledge base 
Customer support bot | Handle common support questions | No external service connections 

### When to Use Which

Question | Instance Per Customer | Session Per User 
---|---|---
Does each user connect their own social/ad/email accounts? | Yes | No 
Do credentials differ between users? | Yes | No 
Is conversation the primary interaction? | Sometimes | Always 
Does the agent perform actions on behalf of the user? | Yes | Rarely 
How many instances do you need? | One per customer | One total (or a few) 

### Hybrid Pattern

A single product can combine both: a per-customer action agent plus a shared conversational agent sit side by side in the same frontend. For example:

- One Social Manager instance per customer (Pattern 1) to publish posts with their own connected social accounts (System User or OAuth, depending on the provider).
- One shared knowledge-base chat agent (Pattern 2) that answers product, billing, or onboarding questions across all customers, usingsessionkey to keep each user's chat separate.

The two agents are independent deployments with differentuseragentguid values. Route user actions to the per-customer instance, and chat questions to the shared instance. Your backend decides which agent handles each request.

## Building Your Product

### White-Label Chat

Build a fully branded chat experience with no Wiro UI visible to your users.

The deploy flow has three stages: Deploy, Setup (only when the agent has connectors to set up), and Start.

- Deploy an agent viaPOST /UserAgent/Deploy: returns useragents[0].guid and starts the instance in status: 6 (setup-required). A prepaid Deploy then queues it (status: 2) once its subscription is provisioned.
- Setup the connectors (only if the agent template requires them) via one or morePOST /UserAgent/CredentialUpsert calls, POST /UserAgent/CredentialProjectBind for the Wiro project, and the matching OAuth flows (see Agent Credentials & OAuth). These calls don't change status: on an agent still at status: 6, call POST /UserAgent/Update with { "guid": "<useragent-guid>" } after the last one and check setuprequired on its response. While it's true, the agent cannot start. Once all required connectors are set up, that call flips setuprequired to false and status to 0. For Pattern 2 (knowledge-base / chat-only agents) there are no connectors to set up, so this stage is skipped and the agent is ready to start right after Deploy.
- Start: a prepaid Deploy already queued the agent, and it goes throughstatus: 3 (starting) → status: 4 (running). Call POST /UserAgent/Start when it is stopped (status: 0, for example after Update moved it out of status: 6) or errored (status: 5).
- Build your own chat UI.
- Send messages viaPOST /UserAgent/Message/Send.
- Stream responses in real-time via Agent WebSocket using theagenttoken.
- Manage conversation history withPOST /UserAgent/Message/History.

See Agent Overview for the full lifecycle state table (status: 0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6).
# Deploy — prepaid + tier are required for API users (credits debit from your wallet)
curl -X POST "https://api.wiro.ai/v1/UserAgent/Deploy" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "agentguid": "agent-template-guid",
    "title": "Customer Support Bot",
    "useprepaid": true,
    "tier": "starter"
  }'

# Pattern 1 only — fill any missing credentials, then verify setuprequired flipped to false

  -d '{ "guid": "deployed-useragent-guid" }'

curl -X POST "https://api.wiro.ai/v1/UserAgent/Start" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: YOUR_API_KEY" \

cross_cutting.content:
## DEV Community

📅 November 13, 2026 • Source: Decagon

Decagon introduced Missions on November 12, 2026, per the company's blog post from product manager Gunguk Kim and member of technical staff Jian Yang. Missions are long-horizon agentic tasks: the agent coordinates work across systems, tracks statuses and engages several people until the outcome is reached, over days or weeks rather than a single exchange. Coverage from unite.ai frames the launch the same way, as Decagon expanding its agents into end-to-end customer workflows.

Setup happens in plain language, per the company: a team states the goal in ordinary words, names the personas involved and adds rules for how to proceed. The agent then carries that goal as a north star and selects the next step on its own until the result lands, whether the horizon runs to days, weeks or months. Orchestration is multi-persona: the agent connects threads across participants, chooses a relevant channel for each of them, and any step that depends on a third party puts the mission on pause until that external side completes its part.

Browser Actions push the work into the back office, for example filling out forms, per the company. The worked example is a prescription renewal: the patient receives a notification, a physician is engaged to authorize the renewal, claims are re-run inside the payer's system, and dispensing details are confirmed back to the patient. Other examples named by the company and by unite.ai include prior authorization for an MRI, approval of a small loan, and lead qualification for sales teams.

Every mission is written down as an Agent Operating Procedure, or AOP: the team writes, edits and tests the logic itself, every agent decision stays visible, and parts of the configuration can be tested before anything ships, per the company. Context comes from two layers — the mission case, a dynamic record of progress and new information, and Memory, which holds preferences such as not calling a customer after 3 PM.

Before each action the agent re-checks the case and Memory and adapts when a customer changes the sequence, for example by booking a follow-up over email on their own, per the company. Duet Autopilot, a Decagon product, adds recommendations for improving the whole route rather than individual interactions. The market framing comes from analyst Futurum: in the segment Missions addresses, 56.5% of enterprise decision-makers name support and customer experience as the top GenAI use case, per Futurum.

IMPACT: For CX teams the practical shift is from tracking statuses and handoffs toward improving each step of a mission, since the agent carries the thread across systems and people over days. Visibility into the AOP doubles as an audit trail for agent decisions. The company itself notes the approach depends on integrations and human oversight, so rollout quality will vary from one deployment to the next.

# [PRNewswire] Gcore and TengriAI to explore 100 MW AI data center

Press Releases 09:04 November 13, 2026

-- Phased project would give Central Asia large-scale GPU capacity run in the region

LUXEMBOURG and ASTANA, Kazakhstan Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire=YONHAP/ -- Gcore and TengriAI have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to explore a GPU data center in Kazakhstan with a target capacity of up to 100 MW, phased between 2027 and 2029.

Central Asia has little domestic AI compute, so organizations depend on capacity in Europe, the Gulf or East Asia, often outside regulatory jurisdiction.

"Every market we work in is asking the same question: how do we run AI on our own terms?" says Andre Reitenbach, CEO of Gcore. "The project would put large-scale GPU infrastructure in the country, operated from the country, for customers across the region."

Under the MoU, TengriAI would handle land, power, permitting and construction. Gcore would provide the AI cloud stack, operations and customer demand. The platform is the one Gcore runs in its own GPU clouds as an NVIDIA Preferred Cloud Partner. Customers could meter, bill and resell capacity, or run isolated workloads that never leave the facility.

"Our goal is to make Kazakhstan a leading AI token hub in Central Asia," said Nurassyl Medeu, General Director of TengriAI. "Gcore operates GPU clouds at scale and has done this with telecom operators."

Gcore is one of few Europe-headquartered companies that operates its own GPU clouds, owns the global network and secures every deployment. "Software vendors have never operated a platform. Hyperscalers will not hand over the keys. We do both," said Reitenbach.

Kazakhstan offers competitively priced energy, available land, lower cooling costs and a government that treats AI infrastructure as a national priority. Its location and the Astana International Financial Centre's common-law framework make it a natural base for neighboring markets.

# Kazakhstan partners explore a data centre of up to 100 MW

Gcore and TengriAI signed an agreement to explore an AI data centre of up to 100 MW in Kazakhstan, with a possible phased rollout from 2027 to 2029.

Gcore, a Luxembourg-based provider of cloud computing, networking and security services, and TengriAI, a Kazakh company developing AI computing infrastructure and a marketplace for AI services, announced on 12 November 2026 that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore developing and operating an AI data centre in Kazakhstan. The companies are considering a facility with a capacity of up to 100 megawatts, with a possible phased rollout from 2027 to 2029. The facility would use graphics processing units (GPUs) to run demanding AI workloads for customers across Central Asia.

Under the proposed arrangement, TengriAI would handle land, power, permits, and construction, while Gcore would provide and operate the cloud platform and bring in customers. Gcore would use the same platform it runs in its existing GPU cloud services. Customers could track usage, bill for it, and resell computing capacity. They could also run isolated workloads that stay within the facility.

Gcore said limited AI computing capacity in Central Asia has led organisations to rely on infrastructure in Europe, the Gulf, and East Asia. The company cited energy prices, available land and lower cooling costs as reasons for exploring a facility in Kazakhstan. It also pointed to the country’s location as an advantage for serving neighbouring markets. TengriAI said its goal is to make Kazakhstan a regional hub for AI computing.

## Why does it matter?

If built, the data centre would give organisations in Central Asia another place to run large AI workloads closer to home. Hosting in Kazakhstan would give customers more choice over where their data is processed and which jurisdiction applies. That choice matters when organisations weigh access to computing capacity alongside requirements on where particular data can be handled. The proposal shows how a facility in one country could serve neighbouring markets while giving customers an alternative to computing infrastructure outside the region.

cross_cutting.content:
Intel has launched a new initiative to strengthen South Korea's AI ecosystem, bringing together hardware, software and service providers to build capabilities across the technology stack.
The company unveiled the K-AI Full-stack Alliance at the 2026 Intel AI Summit Seoul, held at COEX in Seoul's Samseong-dong district on Nov. 12. The alliance launched with 23 participating companies, including Intel, Rebellions, DEEPX, LG AI Research, Upstage, MegazoneCloud and Lablup.
The alliance aims to build a collaborative ecosystem spanning the full AI stack, from chips and hardware to models, software, cloud infrastructure and platforms. It plans to respond to rapidly evolving technologies and customer needs while strengthening capabilities in areas such as sovereign AI—AI developed and operated under national control—and physical AI, which enables machines to perceive and act in the real world. It also seeks to strengthen an AI ecosystem built around Korean-made servers, contributing to the country's broader AI competitiveness.

“South Korea combines strong semiconductor and R&D capabilities with significant potential for innovation in sovereign AI, physical AI and the intelligent edge,” said Santosh Viswanathan, Intel's Asia Pacific regional leader. “Drawing on our open approach to heterogeneous computing and broad AI portfolio, Intel will work with Korea's innovative companies and partners to develop new AI use cases and scale them into larger markets.”
Heterogeneous computing combines different types of processors to handle workloads more efficiently, while intelligent edge systems process data and run AI close to where data is generated.
The Intel AI Summit Seoul brought together domestic and international partners to share Intel's AI strategy, showcase recent innovations and discuss the industry's direction. This year's event drew 52 companies, including Lenovo, LG Electronics, SK hynix, SK Telecom and Samsung Electronics, alongside four government and public-sector organizations: the Ministry of SMEs and Startups, the National IT Industry Promotion Agency (NIPA), the Korea Institute of Startup & Entrepreneurship Development and Seoul AI Hub.
“AI is no longer confined to a particular technology or industry. It is expanding across PCs, data centers, the edge and robotics,” said Tae-won Bae, country manager of Intel Korea. “Intel will work closely with Korean partners and the government to help businesses translate AI's potential into tangible business results and contribute to the growth of Korea's AI ecosystem.”

# Intel Forms AI Alliance With 23 Korean Companies

## K-AI Full Stack Alliance launched at Intel AI Summit Seoul 2026 to target sovereign AI with Korean-made servers

Intel is joining forces with 23 South Korean companies to build AI infrastructure tailored to the Korean market.

The company has launched an alliance spanning hardware, software and AI services, centered on domestically manufactured servers powered by Intel chips. Together with Korean partners, Intel aims to target the sovereign AI and physical AI markets.

Tae-Won Bae, president of Intel Korea, announced the launch at the Intel AI Summit Seoul 2026, held at COEX in Seoul on Nov. 11. “Today marks the official launch of the K-AI Full Stack Alliance,” Bae said. “It represents our commitment to creating innovation together with Korean companies on an open infrastructure and ecosystem built around domestically manufactured servers.” He added that Intel would work closely with local partners and the government to support the development of Korea’s AI ecosystem.

The K-AI Full Stack Alliance is a broad coalition of domestic AI companies centered on Intel. It was established to build a comprehensive AI ecosystem in Korea, covering the entire technology stack. The alliance held its launch ceremony at the event, with 23 initial participants, including KTNF, Dnotitia, Panmnesia, Upstage, Nota AI, DEEPX, FuriosaAI and Exina.

Alliance members will collaborate across the AI industry, including hardware, software, industry-specific AI solutions and services. The partnership aims to strengthen their ability to respond quickly and flexibly to the rapidly evolving AI market. Ultimately, the companies plan to build AI infrastructure using domestically designed servers, contributing to Korea’s sovereign AI capabilities.

Intel Korea will also sign a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Seoul AI Hub to strengthen the technological competitiveness and support the growth of domestic AI startups. The two organizations will help promising Korean AI startups enhance their development capabilities and expand opportunities for technical collaboration.

Other senior Intel executives also took the stage to share the company’s AI technology strategy and examples of innovation.

Santosh Viswanathan, Intel’s Asia-Pacific regional head, identified sovereign AI, personalized AI and edge AI as three areas where Korea could capitalize on emerging opportunities.

“Korea has numerous companies innovating in domestically developed large language models (LLMs), memory and infrastructure,” Viswanathan said. “Korea is particularly well positioned in personal and edge AI, which will create significant business opportunities for all of us.”

Dan Rodriguez, executive vice president and general manager of Intel’s Edge Computing Group, discussed how AI is expanding beyond PCs into edge computing and industrial environments. He also emphasized collaboration among hardware, software and ecosystem partners to deliver AI innovation in real-world settings.

“Intel is building an open AI ecosystem and a foundation of trusted partnerships while providing developers and partners with the tools they need,” Rodriguez said. “For example, Intel Core Ultra Series 3 is a system-on-chip (SoC) integrating multiple processing units, delivering seamless optimization and high performance per watt to meet the needs of edge customers.”

Anil Nanduri, head of AI product go-to-market at Intel’s Data Center AI Group, introduced the company’s server product lineup. Intel is mass-producing Clearwater Forest, a Xeon server processor featuring up to 288 high-density, energy-efficient E-cores. Next year, the company plans to launch Diamond Rapids, featuring up to 256 high-performance P-cores.

Intel also unveiled a physical chip from its next-generation data center inference accelerator lineup, the Intel GPU D-Series. The high-efficiency accelerator delivers up to 26,200 TFLOPS of FP4 performance while consuming 350 watts of power. Compared with the competing Nvidia RTX 6000 Pro, Intel demonstrated advantages including 30% lower latency on Gemma models, 2.2 times higher AI agent performance and up to 5.9 times higher computing performance in financial simulations.
